extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary critics, and advanced students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and executing the 'panoramic' (pictorial) versus the 'scenic' (dramatic) method in novels: handling point of view, time, selection of detail, preparation and presentation of climactic scenes, and authenticating the narrator's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panoramic (pictorial) vs Scenic (dramatic) presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between the 'panoramic' (pictorial) method and the 'scenic' (dramatic) presentation of a story; panorama = broad survey, authorial reminiscence and summary; scenic = immediate, enacted scenes presented to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the terms as technical opposites: panoramic works range over a landscape of life and present a continuous flow of leisurely, contemplative reminiscence (example: Thackeray); scenic/dramatic works put action before us and let characters act for themselves (example: Maupassant). Be aware the line is not mathematically exact, but choose the dominant method consciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose panorama for stories whose point is an impression of a world
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject is an 'impression of a world, a society, a time' (manners within a locale) the panoramic method is appropriate: the book is 'the story which they unite to tell' rather than the story of any single character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the novel's unity depends on a general effect or social panorama rather than an intricate plot, favor summary, survey, and widely sampled detail. Example: Vanity Fair's unity comes from the crowd of typical figures rather than tightly woven intrigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity through typicality rather than plot complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: In panoramic work, unity often 'depends in truth upon one fact only, the fact that all his throng of men and women are strongly, picturesquely typical of the world from which they are taken.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters collectively contribute to a single impression of milieu or manners; a light tie between paths is sufficient for unity. Avoid forcing intricate plot links when the aim is an impressionistic portrait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leisurely, contemplative reminiscence as method
rubrics_metrics.description: Panoramic narration often takes the form of a long retrospective vision—'a continuous flow of leisurely, contemplative reminiscence'—where the author's memory gathers details and presents them in a broad sweep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use retrospective voice, associative recollection, and loose chronology to evoke tone and atmosphere. Let small incidents 'spring up in his mind' as illustrative rather than make them the center of dramatized action.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a climax requires immediate enactment, show it directly
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain final or decisive scenes 'cannot be recalled and summarized in his indirect, reminiscential manner. It must be placed immediately before us' — dramatic enactment is prescribed for real emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize moments that need ocular, present display (e.g., collapse, catastrophe, decisive confrontation). Convert summary into a full scene when the force of the answer to a central question depends on direct presentation. Anti-pattern: compressing the climax into authorial summary weakens its impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare scenically presented climaxes adequately
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene given in dramatic terms must be prepared; insufficient preparation forces theatrical or crude devices and an unnatural effort from characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure earlier parts render characters in terms that can sustain dramatic autonomy; avoid leaving a scene 'insufficiently prepared' so the author is compelled to 'force their note' and produce an 'artificial look.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshortening, generalizing, and fusion of detail for pictorial effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of the pictorial art include 'that foreshortening and generalizing, that fusion of detail, that subordination of the instance and the occasion to the broad effect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subordinate isolated incidents to the overall impression; use suggestion, hints, and brief glimpses ('a hint, a moment, a glance suffices') rather than elaborate scenes when the goal is a broad, harmonious picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting and deploying illustrative incidents sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick scraps of talk and 'tell-tale incidents' that 'illustrate what he has to say' and 'spring up in his mind as he reviews the past.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incidents as reinforcing illustrations—brush past them without overparticularizing. A small, well-chosen detail can enrich the panorama; avoid lingering on incidental scenes that interrupt the overall tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undue authorial intrusion; account for the narrator's authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Panoramic narration often foregrounds the narrator ('we need him all the time'); if the authorial eye remains unaccountable the book can seem inconclusive—'there is an inconclusive look, something that draws the eye away from the book itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either control and justify the narrator's presence or make the point of view objectively part of the work. Failure to account for the narrator's authority leaves loose ends; prudent novelists avoid straining the convention of omniscience unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the seeing eye or incorporate point of view into the story
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'authenticate his story' the novelist may 'dramatize the seeing eye'—making the point of view definite and verifiable in the book (e.g., Flaubert blending his vision with Emma's so her perspective governs the story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the panoramic method risks exposing an unaccountable narrator, adopt techniques to internalize or dramatize the vantage point (e.g., align authorial vision with a character's perception, present narrator as a recognizable presence), thereby making the seeing eye part of the fiction's facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance picture and drama; avoid inconsistent mixing
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture (panorama) and drama are antithetical manners; poor mixing can obscure dramatic occasions or make dramatic passages look artificial ('to give the succession of incident a hard, particular, dramatic relief would be to obscure it').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which mode dominates and maintain coherence. If you shift from panoramic summary to scenic enactment, do so with clear justification and technical readiness; inconsistent switches can produce artificial tone or diminish both effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-handling: use chronology and focus to create 'time' as sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Time can be represented not only as movement but as 'tranquillity'—'time that stands still'—achieved by leisurely play with chronology and shifting the focus so description stores up 'quiet layers of time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ deliberate non-linear ordering, returns, and delays to produce a sense of accumulated time. For work aiming at 'time-pictures' (e.g., Esmond), prioritize depth and duration over strict sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct, ocular proof for lifting dramatic moments
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief, immediate scene can 'lift the story forward dramatically; ocular proof, as it were, is added to the account'—a small enacted moment can provide decisive verification of prior narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert concise, vivid scenes (glimpses) when you want to convert author's summary into evidence the reader can verify visually. Example: Becky seated at the piano gives immediate dramatic proof of her position in society; such moments are short but potent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use flashes of revelation sparingly; they are intense fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: Flashes of revelation ('these flashes of revelation, straight and sure') are powerful but are 'always a fragment, never to any real purpose a deliberate and continuous enactment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ such flashes for high intensity and memorable image-making, but do not rely on them alone to supply necessary continuous enactment or narrative structure; integrate them thoughtfully into either a panoramic or dramatic framework.
